title: Functions, derivatives, and Jacobians: how change propagates

blocks.text: The practical use of derivatives is not isolated limit exercises. Derivatives predict change. If joint angles change slightly, in which direction and by how much does the end-effector move? If a loss grows, which parameter should change? Derivatives and Jacobians make these questions locally computable and connect kinematics, control, optimization, visual servoing, and machine learning.

blocks.text: 3.1 A function: a derivative needs inputs, outputs, and units

A function $y=f(x)$ maps an object from an input space to an output space. Forward kinematics is a function: joint angles $q$ pass through the mechanism to produce end-effector position $p$. Without the input, output, frame, and units of a function, its derivative has no object to describe.

Thus $\partial p/\partial q$ has units m/rad; it is not a unitless matrix. Unit analysis prevents errors in control gains, normalization, and simulation interfaces. Treating an m/rad Jacobian as m/deg changes the scale by $180/\pi$.

blocks.text: 3.2 One-variable derivatives: local slope and prediction
For a scalar function, the derivative describes the local slope:
The engineering prediction is the first-order approximation:

For $f(x)=x^2+2x$ at $x=1.5$, $f'(1.5)=5$. An input increase of $0.01$ predicts an output increase of about $0.05$; the second-order term determines the error. State this prediction before writing the limit definition.

With a large $h$, neglected higher-order terms cause truncation error. With a small $h$, subtracting nearly equal function values amplifies floating-point roundoff. The error usually decreases and then rises. This balance between approximation and numerical error returns in finite-difference Jacobians, gradient checks, and simulation integration.
3.3 Multivariable functions: partial, directional, and Jacobian derivatives
When both input and output are vectors, the derivative is a linear map rather than a scalar. For $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$, near $x$

blocks.latex:
f(x+\Delta x)\approx f(x)+J_f(x)\Delta x,\qquad
  J_f(x)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}.

blocks.text: Column $j$ is the output change caused by moving along input basis direction $e_j$; row $i$ describes the sensitivity of output $i$ to all input components. This is exactly the matrix interpretation from Chapter 2.
is the directional derivative along $v$. It answers “what instantaneous end-effector velocity results from joint velocity $v$?” rather than “what happens when one variable changes in isolation.”
3.4 A 2R arm: deriving forward kinematics from geometry
Consider a planar two-revolute-joint arm with link lengths $l_1,l_2$ and joint angles $q_1,q_2$. The absolute direction of the second link is $q_1+q_2$, so the end position is the sum of two vectors:
Do not memorize this as a standard answer. Draw the two links, project each onto $x$ and $y$, and add them. Different joint conventions may change signs, but the geometric reasoning remains.

blocks.code:
def fk_2r(q, link_lengths=(0.5, 0.35)):
    q = np.asarray(q, dtype=float)
    if q.shape != (2,):
        raise ValueError(f"q must have shape (2,), got {q.shape}")
    l1, l2 = link_lengths
    q1, q2 = q
    q12 = q1 + q2
    return np.array([
        l1*np.cos(q1) + l2*np.cos(q12),
        l1*np.sin(q1) + l2*np.sin(q12),
    ])

blocks.text: 3.5 Deriving the Jacobian: each column is one joint's local effect
Differentiate $p(q)$ with respect to $q_1$ and $q_2$:

blocks.latex:
J(q)=\frac{\partial p}{\partial q}=
\begin{bmatrix}
-l_1\sin q_1-l_2\sin(q_1+q_2) & -l_2\sin(q_1+q_2)\\
l_1\cos q_1+l_2\cos(q_1+q_2) & l_2\cos(q_1+q_2)
\end{bmatrix}.

blocks.text: The first column contains both links because $q_1$ rotates both; the second contains only the second link because $q_2$ changes only the relative angle. This physical interpretation matters more than copying the formula into a matrix.

blocks.title: One column answers one control question

blocks.text: 若 $q=[0.4,-0.7]^T$，取 $\dot q=[0.2,-0.1]^T$ rad/s，则 $J(q)\dot q$ 是末端的瞬时线速度。若只把 $\dot q_1$ 设为非零，$J$ 的第一列直接告诉你末端沿哪一个方向运动；这就是速度层控制器和视觉伺服中“列的意义”。
3.6 The chain rule: from local coordinates to complex models
Robotic systems are compositions: a sensor maps state to features, a policy maps features to actions, and a controller maps actions to joint commands. If $z=g(x)$ and $y=f(z)$, then

blocks.latex:
\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}
  =\frac{\partial y}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}.

blocks.text: This explains two things. First, backpropagation is the chain rule organized on a computation graph, not a new kind of magic. Second, robot transform and Jacobian chains must match intermediate spaces; multiplying a Jacobian in one frame by a velocity in another is a malformed chain rule.
3.7 Verify the Jacobian with finite differences: test the approximation
The analytic derivation gives

A verification should track three things: whether the step is small enough, whether the error decreases with the step, and whether numerical sensitivity appears near singular configurations. Comparing one output array only proves that one call did not crash.

blocks.code:
def jacobian_2r(q, link_lengths=(0.5, 0.35)):
    q1, q2 = np.asarray(q, dtype=float)
    l1, l2 = link_lengths
    s12, c12 = np.sin(q1+q2), np.cos(q1+q2)
    return np.array([
        [-l1*np.sin(q1)-l2*s12, -l2*s12],
        [ l1*np.cos(q1)+l2*c12,  l2*c12],
    ])

def finite_difference_jacobian(q, h=1e-6):
    q = np.asarray(q, dtype=float)
    result = np.empty((2, 2))
    for j in range(2):
        direction = np.zeros(2)
        direction[j] = h
        result[:, j] = (fk_2r(q+direction)-fk_2r(q-direction))/(2*h)
    return result

q = np.array([0.4, -0.7])
analytic = jacobian_2r(q)
numerical = finite_difference_jacobian(q)
assert np.linalg.norm(analytic-numerical) < 1e-8

blocks.text: 3.8 Singularity and conditioning: which task directions are difficult
When the columns of $J$ become nearly linearly dependent, the two joint effects point in nearly the same direction and some end-effector motions become difficult. For the planar 2R arm,

Thus the arm is singular when $q_2=0$ or $\pi$, where it is straight or folded. Numerically, singular values $\sigma_{\max},\sigma_{\min}$ and the condition number $\kappa=\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}$ are more robust indicators. They can be monitored as controller safety signals.

blocks.title: A singularity is not a coding bug

blocks.text: Near a singularity, the inverse Jacobian may turn a small Cartesian velocity request into huge joint velocities. Increasing speed limits turns geometric uncontrollability into collision risk. Reduce task speed, use a damped pseudoinverse, change the posture, or replan.
3.9 Inverse differential kinematics: from task velocity to joint velocity
To achieve a task velocity $v$, the ideal relation is $J\dot q=v$. If $J$ is invertible, $\dot q=J^{-1}v$; more generally use the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse $J^\dagger$:
Near a singularity use a damped pseudoinverse:

Damping introduces bias but limits velocity amplification. A larger $\lambda$ is not always safer because it reduces task tracking accuracy. Schedule it from singular values, joint speed limits, and task tolerance.
3.10 Turn the rate map into a control experiment: discrete time and safety
A rate-level controller is not yet a complete control system. A discrete implementation needs a sampling period $\Delta t$:
A minimal point controller sets $e=p_{goal}-p(q)$, requests $v=Ke$, and maps it through the damped pseudoinverse. It must additionally check joint limits, speed clipping, collisions, and singularity.

blocks.code:
def move_to_target(q0, target, steps=500, dt=0.01):
    q = np.asarray(q0, dtype=float).copy()
    target = np.asarray(target, dtype=float)
    history = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        position = fk_2r(q)
        error = target - position
        history.append((q.copy(), position.copy(), error.copy()))
        if np.linalg.norm(error) < 1e-4:
            break
        velocity = 3.0 * error
        qdot, _, condition = resolved_rate_step(
            q, velocity, damping=0.02, max_joint_speed=1.0)
        if condition > 1e3:
            raise RuntimeError("near-singular configuration")
        q = q + dt*qdot
        q = np.clip(q, [-np.pi, -np.pi], [np.pi, np.pi])
    return q, history

blocks.text: Failure in this experiment does not mean the Jacobian method is invalid. Record whether failure came from an unreachable target, a singular start, speed clipping, joint limits, or a large time step. A research report should separate these causes.
3.11 Automatic differentiation and gradient checks: a shared language

Automatic differentiation obtains derivatives from a computation graph using the chain rule; it is not symbolic differentiation and is not finite differences. Finite differences remain valuable as an independent numerical sanity check. For a new loss or Jacobian, compare autodiff and finite differences on small fixed inputs before training or control.

blocks.code:
import torch

q = torch.tensor([0.4, -0.7], dtype=torch.double, requires_grad=True)
l1, l2 = 0.5, 0.35
position = torch.stack((
    l1*torch.cos(q[0]) + l2*torch.cos(q[0]+q[1]),
    l1*torch.sin(q[0]) + l2*torch.sin(q[0]+q[1]),
))
loss = (position**2).sum()
gradient, = torch.autograd.grad(loss, q)
assert gradient.shape == (2,)

blocks.text: If autodiff disagrees with the analytic expression, first check tensor shapes, broadcasting, angle units, accidental detachment, and whether the loss is the intended physical quantity. “It backpropagates” does not mean “the gradient is correct.”
3.12 Failure cases: a correct derivative can still fail

items: Local model out of range: a large step invalidates $J(q)\Delta q$; relinearize or reduce the step.
Frame mismatch: multiplying a base-frame Jacobian by a tool-frame velocity can be numerically stable but physically wrong.
Unit mismatch: degrees may enter a radian function, or mm may enter an m/rad Jacobian.
Singularity: a pseudoinverse amplifies noise and speed; use damping, limits, or posture planning.
Discrete instability: a good continuous-time law may diverge with a large $\Delta t$.
Unreachable: outside the workspace, control can only compromise.

blocks.text: Check units and frames first; verify forward kinematics on a hand-computable pose; compare analytic and finite-difference Jacobians; inspect singular values and speed; only then tune gains or network structure.

blocks.title: Oral template: what does a Jacobian do in robotics?

blocks.text: The Jacobian is the first-order local linearization of forward kinematics. Column $j$ is the local end-effector velocity contribution of joint $j$, so $\dot p=J(q)\dot q$. Near a singularity, some task directions require very large joint velocities, so the controller needs damping, limits, or replanning.
3.15 Cross-Part linearization evidence: do not merely trust $J\delta q$

At this point, a derivative or Jacobian should not remain a formula that can merely be written down. It is a local model: near the current $q$, $J(q)\delta q$ predicts the actual endpoint displacement. Research use asks one more question: for which step sizes, postures, and task directions is that local model trustworthy? This section turns the Taylor remainder into measurable evidence rather than an abstract higher-order term.

For smooth forward kinematics and a non-degenerate direction, the absolute remainder is usually $O(h^2)$ and the relative error is usually $O(h)$. This is not a promise that every implementation must produce slope one: near singular postures, angle branches, clipping, or noise can change the slope. Report the observed slope, endpoint residual (m), step (rad), and $\sigma_{\min}(J)$ (m/rad), together with the validity range.

blocks.title: 2R 手算与证据 / Hand calculation and evidence for a 2R arm

blocks.text: Take $q=[0.4,-0.7]$ rad and $v=[1,-0.4]/\|[1,-0.4]\|$. At $h=0.1$ rad, the actual displacement is about $0.062416$ m, the linear prediction $0.062610$ m, the residual $0.002590$ m, and the relative error $0.04150$. At $h=0.001$ rad, the residual falls to $2.59\times10^{-7}$ m and the relative error to $4.14\times10^{-4}$. The log--log slope over five steps is about $1.0003$, while $\sigma_{\min}=0.1306$ m/rad and the condition number is about $6.61$. Shrinking the step and avoiding an ill-conditioned posture are two separate dimensions of evidence.

blocks.code:
from linearization_evidence_lab import (
    local_linearization_sweep, observed_relative_error_order,
    task_loss_report,
)

records = local_linearization_sweep(
    q=[0.4, -0.7], direction=[1.0, -0.4])
order = observed_relative_error_order(records)
assert order > 0.7                 # evidence, not a universal law
assert records[-1]["linearization_residual_m"] < 1e-5

report = task_loss_report([0.4, -0.7], target=[0.65, 0.15])
assert report["jacobian_m_per_rad"].shape == (2, 2)
assert report["gauss_newton_hessian_m2_per_rad2"].shape == (2, 2)

blocks.title: 同一个局部模型如何流向后续章节 / How the same local model flows forward

blocks.text: Chapter 29's MPC should not merely write down $A_k,B_k$; use the residual growth with $h$ to choose relinearization frequency, prediction horizon, and trust-region radius. Chapter 39's image Jacobian needs the same calibration for the local radius of “pixel change versus endpoint velocity”, combined with observation age, covariance, and the minimum singular value to decide whether to servo. Chapter 69's Gauss--Newton Hessian $J^TJ$ turns the same Jacobian into loss curvature and reveals directions amplified by data or geometry.

blocks.title: 一次小步验证不等于全局可信 / One small-step check is not global validity

blocks.text: A small error at one posture, direction, and step does not establish global validity for a controller or MPC model. Vary posture, direction, step, frame, and noise; label contact-mode switches, joint limits, angle wrapping, and visual occlusion separately. Near a singularity, the Taylor residual may be small while $J^\dagger$ still amplifies speed and noise. That is why local-approximation error and inverse-problem conditioning must be reported together.

blocks.title: 本节练习与答案提示 / Exercises and answer cues

items: Why is the theoretical order of relative error usually one lower than that of the absolute residual?
Add $q=[0,0]$ to the sweep and compare $\sigma_{\min}$, condition number, and error slope.
Explain why MPC should relinearize when model residual exceeds a threshold instead of merely increasing solver iterations.

blocks.text: Answer cues: actual displacement is first order while the Taylor remainder is second order; the straight posture has nearly zero $\sigma_{\min}$ and an ill-conditioned inverse; a solver can solve a wrong local model more accurately but cannot repair an invalid model range.
3.16 Completion standard and research exit

Minimum evidence: hand-derive one term of 2R forward kinematics; explain each Jacobian column; run the analytic/finite-difference comparison; run `test_linearization_evidence_lab.py` and report the observed relative-error order; run a damped pseudoinverse near a singular pose; record one controller failure cause; and explain Jacobians, units, and singularities in Chinese and English.

Connect the frame-aware transform from Chapter 2 to this Jacobian in a 2R point-reaching experiment. Record the target, trajectory, end-effector error, peak joint speed, smallest singular value, and failure cause across targets, postures, noise, and control periods.
